Here's the bad news first: This game is maybe 3-4 hours long. The puzzles aren't too terribly hard to figure out and there doesn't seem to be any branching paths to the narrative. Also, the blur effect on the cutscenes could be irritating to some.

The good news: It's a well-told story that IS short, but it's surprisingly punchy. A few of the puzzles are gripping to solve and the story builds consistently with intrigue and suspense as you go. It's all organic and nothing feels out of place. The soundtrack is *superbly* done with music fitting pretty much everything you're doing. 

$14 for 3 hours is kind of a steep ask for a video game, but considering how much it is to go to a movie theater these days and spend more for *less*, your mileage may vary. Worth it on a sale, I'd wager.

Give this one a look! The ending definitely has some hints to a possible sequel and if they make one, I have faith they'll make an even longer game with more to do as this feels almost like a tech demo or a trial run. I want them to really sink in a longer story, more intrigue, more stuff to do, and give us the chance to find a better path than just one single narrative. 

Choice matters to the player and if we feel like nothing we did really changed anything on the main scenario, it can be jarring when the ending piledrives us with how things turned out despite our efforts. Food for thought, Bureau 81!

Anyways, I'm giving this a recommend. Your choice to wait for sale or not, but it's not so steep you won't enjoy yourself with a well-crafted and thought-out experience. Light on gaming, heavy on story and immersion.

[h1][b] TLDR: Sells itself as an investigative puzzler but delivers a mostly on-rails visual novel experience. The handful of genuine puzzles are great, making their scarcity all the more frustrating.
[/b] [/h1]

[h1]PROS: [/h1]
➕Neat investigative puzzles (ENHANCE….ENHANCE)
➕Some nice puzzles, like bomb defuse

[h1]NEUTRALS: [/h1]
🔹Story is good, but a bit too on-rails and hand-holding

[h1]CONS: [/h1]
➖Lots of unskippable intentionally blurry cutscenes leaves a cheap or vague feeling
➖Some reveals are not as big as they should be simply because you wouldn’t know things that your character would know

[h1] [b] Content (Game world/Narrative) – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
The game world takes place entirely from a computer screen and is set in the 90s, we’re talking older CRT monitor screens. There’s not much exploration to be found, as you work for the government and everything is pretty locked down. I’d say the world is a bit basic and simple, only serving as a UI to show some puzzles. 

The narrative has some good parts. You play as Evan Tanner, a Federal Department of Investigation (FDI) operator, in which your job is to assist field agents. You very quickly learn that there’s something going on and you are enlisted, whether you want to or not, to uncover the truth. 
So while I did enjoy the story to an extent, any scene not at the computer and is told through a characters eyes is a blurry mess of objects that are nearly undecipherable. This could be something related to the story, but I don’t want to give the game the benefit of the doubt here and say that it worsens the experience. 

[h1][b] Gameplay (Mechanics/Difficulty) – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The gameplay seems pretty cool at first, but you quickly realize how on-rails the game is. Essentially, this is a glorified visual novel with a few puzzles sprinkled in. At first, I felt like Garcia from Criminal Minds - I was the internet sleuth assisting agents in the field by giving them on-the-fly information to help with cases. But unfortunately, the game isn’t as cool as that. 
The loop consists of you having a conversation, being presented with evidence, and then using the 2-3 tools at your disposal to answer a question presented by the conversation. For example, you’ll need to identify a killer and a victim by scanning their faces to get their names, then look them up in the FDI database. Same thing with licenses plates or analyzing footage/pictures. It does sound very cool, but I can’t emphasize enough the on-rails experience and lack of deep puzzle mechanics. This is more of a game focused on the narrative. 

The difficulty is forgiving. I’m pretty sure I made every wrong choice in the game, yet still made it to the end. I literally messed up a [spoiler]bomb defuse and got an agent killed[/spoiler]. Whoops. Despite these consequences, this doesn’t seem like it impacted the game as much and wasn’t mentioned again other than a few brief times after the fact. 

[h1] [b] Graphics (Quality/Technical) – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
Being that the game is from the point of view of a computer screen and all “Real” scenes are a blurry mess, I’d say the quality isn’t great. What footage you do see is grainy 90’s-era quality, but aside from that the computer UI is good and crisp. 

On the technical side, I had no issues, encountered no bugs, and ran the game without issues. 

1440p @ 240hz | installed on SSD  

[h1] [b] Audio – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The music isn’t really noticeable, but it does increase in intensity during high-drama parts. 

There is a lot of voice acting, and it all sounds good. 

[h1] [b] Replay Factor (Longevity) – [2/10] [/b] [/h1]
Not a lot of replay value here, unless you want to redo the puzzles again for achievements. 

[h1] [b] Final Verdict – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The Operator is described as a game with detective/investigation, and puzzle elements. I’d estimate the game to be about 70% story/narrative focus, 20% puzzles, and 10% deducing or investigating. I’d say that Operator is an okay game, but I was a bit disappointed by the mystery and investigative sides. This is very much a visual novel game more than anything, and as someone that likes visual novels, I was expecting more to use my brain to make deductions instead of clicking pre-defined replies. 

The game does have a few puzzles. I’d say maybe ~10 at the most, and despite that small number, I found them to be good puzzles. Analyzing gunpowder was really cool. Defusing a bomb on the fly was also great. If the game was more focused on gameplay like that, then I’d give it a much higher score, but these are the highest highs that The Operator offers, and there’s only a few of them. 

The real focus of the game is on the narrative. While I wouldn’t consider the narrative to be bad, there were a few parts that were either ridiculously obvious, or a missed opportunity. 
Obvious, because of metagaming - anyone who watches mystery shows knows that there’s only so many characters who could be the culprit due to you the show introducing them to the viewer. Same concept here, it’s obviously going to be the handful of people you know about already. 
Missed opportunity because you as the player only know what you know. One part in particular [spoiler]has the player finding out his apartment is being watched with a camera, and you have to identify whose apartment it is[/spoiler]. Well how can you possibly figure that out without knowing anything about the characters' life, nor ever having been there? Dumb. 

Overall, I do recommend The Operator, but it’s important that you know what you’re going into. This is NOT about deduction or investigating, and that’s not necessarily a bad thing, but I feel the game presents itself in a way that it’s something that it isn’t. 

[h1] [b] Recommend? (Price) [Y/N] [/b] [/h1]
[h1]Yes[/h1]
$14 base price is a bit much for a ~5 hour game with very low replay value. Wait for a sale. Around ~$5-7 would be a good point.

review_text_raw:
The Operator, developed by Bureau 81 and published by Bureau 81 together with indienova, is a tightly focused narrative puzzle game that transforms the quiet, procedural work of intelligence analysis into a tense and engaging thriller. Rather than placing players in the role of an action hero or field agent, the game casts them as a desk-bound operator, someone whose power comes not from physical presence but from information, observation, and deduction. This shift in perspective defines the entire experience, creating a game that feels intimate, cerebral, and deliberately restrained.

You play as Evan Tanner, a newly recruited operator working for the fictional Federal Department of Intelligence. Your job is to support agents in the field by analysing data, processing evidence, and drawing connections that others might miss. The game unfolds almost entirely through Evan’s workstation, presented as a simulated computer desktop filled with databases, analysis tools, messaging systems, and case files. This interface-driven approach immediately sets the tone: instead of cinematic spectacle, The Operator relies on immersion through routine, making the player feel like they are genuinely sitting at a government terminal late at night, piecing together fragments of truth.

Gameplay revolves around solving a series of cases that gradually escalate in complexity and importance. Early tasks feel procedural—identifying suspects, tracing movements, or cross-referencing records—but as the story unfolds, patterns begin to emerge and the stakes rise. Players are required to closely read documents, examine photos and videos, search databases, and interpret subtle clues hidden in plain sight. The puzzles reward attentiveness and logical reasoning, often asking players to synthesize information from multiple sources rather than relying on a single obvious answer. When a breakthrough occurs, it feels earned, the result of careful thought rather than trial and error.

As the narrative progresses, the game shifts from isolated casework into a broader conspiracy. A mysterious hacker begins to interfere with FDI systems, raising questions about surveillance, authority, and the reliability of the information you’re working with. This transition adds narrative tension without abandoning the game’s grounded tone. The story remains largely linear, but it is effectively paced, allowing suspense to build gradually as seemingly unrelated assignments reveal deeper connections. Dialogue and character interactions are understated, delivered through calls, messages, and system prompts rather than dramatic cutscenes, which reinforces the feeling that you are always working behind the scenes.

One of the game’s greatest strengths is how convincingly it uses its interface as both a storytelling and gameplay tool. Every window, search bar, and analysis program feels purposeful, and learning how to use these tools becomes part of the experience. While some mechanics are simplified or exaggerated for gameplay purposes, they remain believable within the fiction, maintaining immersion. The design encourages players to slow down, double-check assumptions, and think critically—mistakes often stem from overlooking details rather than misunderstanding mechanics.

Visually, The Operator embraces a minimalist, utilitarian aesthetic inspired by older operating systems and institutional software. The interface is dense but readable, intentionally lacking visual flair in favor of authenticity. This design choice may feel dry to some players, but it suits the game’s themes perfectly, emphasizing bureaucracy, control, and the monotony of surveillance work. Subtle audio cues, ambient hums, and restrained music enhance tension without distracting from concentration, allowing the player’s focus to remain on the task at hand.

In terms of pacing, the game strikes a careful balance. It is compact, typically completed in a handful of hours, but it avoids feeling rushed. Each case builds naturally on the last, and the increasing narrative weight keeps momentum strong. The linear structure limits replayability, as choices rarely branch into significantly different outcomes, but this also allows the developers to maintain tight narrative control and deliver a coherent, focused story without filler.

Community reception reflects appreciation for the game’s originality and execution. Players who enjoy detective work, mystery narratives, and “games on a computer” style experiences frequently praise its atmosphere and puzzle design. Criticism tends to focus on its short length, limited player agency, and occasional moments where immersion is broken by game-like constraints. Even so, these issues rarely overshadow the strengths of the experience, particularly for players aligned with its intended audience.

Taken as a whole, The Operator is a confident and distinctive narrative puzzle game that finds tension in observation rather than action. It succeeds by committing fully to its premise, turning data analysis and desk work into compelling gameplay through thoughtful design and strong thematic focus. While it may not appeal to players seeking open-ended systems or high replay value, it offers a memorable, tightly constructed experience for those who enjoy slow-burn storytelling, logical deduction, and the quiet unease of uncovering truths from behind a screen.

Rating: 9/10

review_text_raw:
The game kind of struggles with what it actually wants you to do and who it wants you to be.

To get started: I really wanted to love this game, because I like researching and playing detective. However you are given a set of tools and expectations to be resourceful, while actually non of it works outside the main storyline. 

As a package it is nicely crafted and for a while it has you engaged, but at some points it expects you to really take control and go beyond the objective ... but only in the exact path the developer(s) have set out for you. The developer(s) haven't realized that it becomes very frustrating, very fast that the game doesn't allow you to explore or make combinations other than that what they exactly have programmed you to do. So encouraging you to think beyond one case, but at the same time limiting your possibilities very much gets your frustrated easily. Sure there is a subpath that you miss sometimes, but you only miss it because all your other attempts to try something different aren't supported (like you can't call anyone on your own or analyse something that isn't supposed to be analyzed). If you don't have any room to play / experiment, you stop doing it and than at some point the game will make fun of you and point out that you have missed something.

Same goes for the dialogs. The game keeps asking you to select an answer while none of it really matters, it is all linear! Again it learns you to make choices, but the choices don't matter so why are they even there than? Just for a single different line of text to go back to the main story path again?

I'll try to give it a go some more when I am less frustrated. But for now, it has got me fed up.

review_text_raw:
The Operator is a 5/10 for me. I just didn’t like it, and the ending honestly pissed me off. It felt dumb. I went into this game thinking I’d be connecting the dots, using my brain, cracking a case, or at least acting like the man in the chair. I expected some detective-style depth, and yeah, I knew there’d be a story, but not this kind of story.

Gameplay & Expectations
I watched the trailer, played the demo, and at first I was excited. The gameplay itself was fun for what it was, and I thought it would build into something bigger. Instead, it just… ended. The ending was surprising, sure, but it wasn’t good. It left me feeling like all that build-up led nowhere.

Replay Value
There’s barely any replay value. No unlimited mode, no side content, nothing to keep you going after finishing the story. And if I remember correctly, there’s not much you can do to actually change the ending, so I had zero motivation to replay it.

Final Thoughts
It’s a fun little game on sale, but I’d recommend watching a video and playing the demo before you consider buying it. Once I beat it, I felt completely done with

review_text_raw:
I have depression. Playing games is one of a few ways I try to take my mind off of things that would typically worsen that depression, something that is proving exceptionally more difficult at the time of this writing. I actively avoid media that would obviously worsen that depression. I keep up on my anti-depression meds. This is how I take care of myself.

People are free to enjoy the media that they enjoy, and some people will, and have, really enjoyed this game. I won't fault people for that. As much as I hate to say it, I think I'm probably a case study for why some things need content warnings, because I'm going to be carrying this game's ending with me now and I really wish I didn't have to carry that on top of everything else I deal with on a day-to-day basis.

That said, I will not be directly spoiling anything. I went in blind, which if you're like me, I strongly advise you not to do. Watch a playthrough, or preferably just read up on the community posts first. Those'll mostly tell you all you need to know whether this is a game you'll be able to enjoy or not.

All that aside, the investigative gameplay was great, but a little lacking. They introduce tools and mechanics you use once and never again, which feels like a lot of wasted potential.

Again, if you're like me and prefer to play games to escape having to dwell on all the problems with real life, I advise you to give this game a pass and instead, pick up Scrutinized and play it on Detective Mode. Similar gameplay without reminding you quite as much about how much you really hate some aspects of the world you live in.

I think if I weren't in the mental state I'm in, I probably would have enjoyed the game more, and even appreciated the ending more. It is certainly realistic. review_text_raw:
I recommend it ... but with some qualifications. 

So, the presentation is excellent. Really builds a strong atmosphere of mystery. There are points when you really feel like you're an operator for a field agent uncovering a major conspiracy. The game does a very good job of doing that. Some of the puzzles took some thinking. They're not super-difficult, but they all make sense in the context of the game and there's not a lot of handholding. Overall, I like how it's all presented.

However ... what I didn't realize is that this is more visual novel than a true puzzle game. It's not a pure visual novel - there is some genuine gameplay here. And that gameplay is pretty good. But ultimately, the gameplay is to trigger the next scene. You can't really "fail" - or at least, you can't fail in a way that will affect the story.

I had believed the game to be a puzzler in the vein of Obra Dinn or Orwell. And I would say the gameplay is as good in part. But after a while, I could "see the rails" - see that at its core, it's a visual novel.

However, that's not why I was disappointed.

The bigger problem I had with the game is that I felt it was ... too short. Not in terms of game length - but in terms of the plot. It felt like it ended right when the plot was getting interesting. 

Putting spoilers on anything further:
[spoiler]Where the game ends, when the intrigue is getting intense and the identity twist is revealed ... I felt almost like that's where the real story is starting. 

Up until this point, our protagonist has just been faceless tech guy who doesn't have a role in the story - and suddenly now we understand how he ties into the conspiracy. And we also understand just what kind of terrible enemy we're up against. 

With this dramatic twist, we now understand the protagonist and his role in the story - as well as true nature and threat of the antagonist that he faces. The stakes have been made clear. The die is cast, the point of no return is reached. 

The question is, what happens now? What does our protagonist do with his new forbidden knowledge? And how can he defeat this terrible enemy?... but instead - the story unceremoniously ends right there. Not only is it kind of a bummer of an ending - but it feels like you stopped telling me this story exactly at the point where it became interesting. Right at the point where things had fully shifted from "Government Bureau Employee Simulator" to "Global Spy Conspiracy Thriller". Our agency has revealed they're evil and they betrayed us, we're gonna go rogue, and take the conspiracy down .... no, wait, actually, that's the end. [/spoiler] 
 
[spoiler]It'd be like if moments after Jason Bourne realized that he was a secret agent and that assassins were trying to kill him ... he just died and the movie ended.

Or, to use a videogame equivalent - it'd be like if right when it's revealed that Doki Doki Literature Club is not actually an anime dating sim ... the game just ended.

There's no resolution. The story feels incomplete. If anything, this feels like it should be the prologue to the real plot. Like a teaser that gives us a glimpse of "OMG these guys are really bad". 

Actually, at the end, when it shifts to HAL's perspective - I thought that was where the real game was about to begin. like, "Twist, Tanner dies in the prologue! You're actually playing as HAL. How will HAL defeat the Organization?" ... But then the credits rolled.[/spoiler] 
 
[spoiler]Part of the problem was that I figured out the twist long before it was revealed. I wasn't being clever, either - it was clear from the opening cutscene that we were not playing as some anonymous rando. We are obviously someone who is involved with this conspiracy in some way. As events played out, the only possibilities were either (a) you were secretly one of the missing people or (b) you were secretly the Ghost. When it became clear you weren't the Ghost ... well, there's only one missing person who we know by name, so that must be you.[/spoiler] 
 
I will say I was thoroughly engaged up until the ending. Even when it started to become clear that the story was more on rails that I'd hoped - I didn't mind because the presentation was so good and the story had me hooked. 

But when it ended ... I felt very disappointed because I was like, "Wait, we're ending it here? That's it?"

So I guess that's my recommend. It's a very well-done experience and the devs clearly were doing something right to keep me gripped. I intended to just try the game for a bit and ended up finishing it in one setting. But it really surprised me that it ended where it did.

review_text_raw:
The Operator offers a remarkably engaging narrative experience, supported by a strong storyline and a well-executed plot twist. The structure of each case is thoughtfully designed: from the call system to the investigative tasks, every step feels purposeful and polished. Working through evidence, analyzing data, and piecing together conclusions is consistently satisfying and stands out as one of the game’s greatest strengths.

Because the investigative tools and the workstation interface are so enjoyable to use, I found myself wishing for a mode that would provide long-term engagement beyond the main story. The campaign can be completed relatively quickly, and once it ends, the gameplay loop—despite being excellent—comes to an abrupt stop.

A dedicated free-play or “ongoing operations” mode could meaningfully extend the game’s lifespan. For example, players could receive procedurally generated cases or scenario-based assignments that scale in complexity, allowing them to continue applying the tools and systems introduced in the main storyline. This would give players who enjoy the investigative process a space to keep refining their skills and exploring the mechanics without a fixed ending.

I am very much looking forward to The Operator 2, and I genuinely believe that adding an optional long-term mode—whether free-play, case generator, or rotating scenario board—would significantly enhance replay value and increase the game’s overall appeal.

For anyone considering this title: the core experience is absolutely worth it, and the investigative gameplay is exceptionally well-crafted. The story alone justifies the €14 price, and I can recommend it without hesitation.

I kind of wish Steam had a neutral option, because there are certain things about this game that are made really well. But overall I decided to get it refunded because it wasn't worth the price for me.

The "puzzles" are really more reading things in order or straight up being given the answer, and you can't even do anything with any other connections you find early on. And speaking of that, you find a LOT early on, because nearly everything is super obvious. There was only one puzzle that I genuinely was impressed with and one tool that I found really cool within another puzzle. Otherwise, the game is very linear even though it seems like it isn't, and nothing you do really matters. You can't make your own decisions or find your own connections between information. The game just walks you through each step and only allows you to do anything with that specific thing at that time.

Other than the somewhat lackluster gameplay, I personally found the ending to be extremely disappointing, because it basically answered everything you already figured out for yourself and answered nothing you didn't. The main story doesn't even really end, it just gets cut off--and in a really unrealistic way, too. It seems to be an obvious sequel setup, but in doing so it doesn't ever truly "end" this game.

The game is also very short, maybe two hours at most. Shorter even than it seems from the reviews. I wouldn't waste my money on it.

Game has good base features, such as databases and interactable video/image search functions, as well as references to certain lab and analysis tools. There was also good voice acting and character designs.
However, I had not realized game was such a railroaded linear story line with no real choices or variation in gameplay. Several points where game takes control from player and forces unnecessary video or audio cutscenes that do not add well to the experience or even the story. Certain events forcibly squish the interactable area of the screen, making it difficult to maneuver through the various game elements needed to continue. Not friendly to slow readers, as whenever a new line of text appears, it forces the log to the bottom, forcing you to wait until the whole conversation is over to double check the one thing you wanted to check in the conversation, such as spelling of a name you want to look up.
Would not recommend for anything more than $4.99

The Operator – 8/10 – A Tense and Captivating Dive into Espionage

The Operator is a stealth-driven, psychological thriller that plunges players into the shadowy world of covert operations, high-stakes intelligence, and moral ambiguity. With an engaging narrative and a compelling atmosphere, it combines tactical gameplay with deep narrative exploration, offering a gripping experience for fans of espionage games. While it may not reinvent the wheel, The Operator does a great job of delivering a tightly-paced, immersive story that keeps you on the edge of your seat.

In The Operator, you play as a field agent working for a secretive government agency, tasked with handling covert missions that blur the lines between right and wrong. The game is heavy on stealth and strategy, as you navigate through a series of complex scenarios—whether infiltrating a heavily guarded facility, gathering intelligence, or neutralizing a threat. The gameplay is tense and slow-paced, with an emphasis on thinking ahead, blending in with your surroundings, and making choices that can lead to either success or failure. It’s all about staying unseen, listening for clues, and using your limited resources wisely. The tension constantly builds as you wonder if you’ll be caught or if the consequences of your decisions will haunt you later on.

The game’s mechanics are simple but effective. You don’t have a full arsenal at your disposal like in many action-heavy titles, and that’s part of the charm. The focus here is on patience, strategy, and managing the few tools you have, whether it’s a silenced pistol or hacking equipment. The difficulty comes not from constant firefights but from the challenge of navigating through dangerous environments, avoiding detection, and managing the relationships and choices you make along the way.

Pretty short overall and that's a little disappointing. My playtime is inflated by leaving it running for a number of hours when I ran off to do other things. But overall fun and interesting. Not bad to grab at this price point.

Plot is pretty interesting and the gameplay is pretty fun. Unfortunately all the cases are exclusively focused on the main plot. It would have been interesting to have things a little more spread out and do either some generic cases or a much beefier plot because it feels like you're aggressively pushed into making bigger plot connections rather than uncovering them on your own. Usually filler is a negative but this game would absolutely have benefited from it. Similarly so for the freedom to explore more connections yourself.

It also struggles a little because you're given a few different tools but they're largely only used for one or two cases. Specifically the chemical analysis capability or bomb defusal but the vehicle one too. It would have been nice to have those elements used more and if there were some filler cases, it would have felt less forced.

It's a unique experience and fun to play. The concept works and I think it could be refined in subsequent games if the developer was so inclined.

review_text_raw: I can't in good conscience give this game a good review, but I also can't give it a poor review. It's times like this I wish Steam had a middle-ground review option. This game was very fun and scratched an itch I didn't know I had. However, labeling it as an investigation game or describing it the way it does is misleading. Yes, there is some investigation, but there's really only one singular crime to solve. The storyline is very linear and easy to guess. If it were marketed as a game about solving a singular crime, that would be accurate, but it misleads you in the description by stating, 'Investigate mysterious crimes. Use cutting-edge FDI software to dig for clues, solve puzzles, and uncover the truth.' This is incorrect. You only use most of the 'software' exactly once, after implying you should read the extensive manual that comes along with it. This is a game that you could probably finish within 2-3 hours, which also doesn't justify its price. Honestly, they could have dropped the mid-tier storyline and just made a game along the lines of Criminal Minds or CSI, where you use these tools to try to solve cases, and it would be infinitely more fun. I know I'm probably the outlier here with my review, and I will say I did enjoy what they had, but it just wasn't what they promised in their wording and descriptions (maybe I misunderstood some stuff, who knows). There does seem to be an open door for expansions in the future, but if they're along the same timeframe as this game and offer only 2-3 hours of playtime, they should drastically reduce the price because as it stands, it felt like an expensive tech demo.

review_text_raw:
[h1] Short and fun little deep state conspiracy game [/h1] 

First of all, this game is short.[b] VERY SHORT [/b]. It takes about 3-4 hours to complete, but the game tells the story it wants to tell in that time so it´s fine. 

[h3] Story 7/10 [/h3] 
The story is fine. It starts of strong, leaving you as the operator to figure out what you are doing and why you are doing it.
As soon as the story picks up the pace, the game is beginning to get more and more predictable. Sure, it makes sure to tell the story in a convincing way, but if the player has had any contact with books that follow similar plotlines or watched a few "rogue agent fighting conspiracy" movies you know where the plot is going and how the game will end. Ending was fine, a bit disappointing because the cut was fast and hard and resulted in a cliff hanger. To me it feels like the devs wrote a story thats about 10 hours long and just cut the game in half when they had the opportunity to do so, preparing the player for a future sequel.

[b] STORY SPOILERS [/b]
[spoiler] In my opinion the reveal that Mike Trench, our friend and FDI director, is the mole and head of the "Operator Program" was very predictable about half-way through  the game (ever since the Biolab incident and the player operator talking about "baiting out the mole"). The Ghost was written in a very stereotypical bad guy hitman way: I dont have a name, my identity was erased. I know the truth but can not tell you. You can ask any question as long as it is not "out of bounds". Yeah, very corny and kinda cringy. In general, even though the way it is written is good and convincing for the most part, sometimes the game feels like the devs wanted to take the easy way out in a few situations (Player being Sasha Cole, Xavier actually being a friend of HAL, the Ghost just escaping like nothing happened and being able to interfere with HALs scripts...) But hey, for what it is, it´s a solid experience. [/spoiler] 

[h3] Music 7/10 [/h3] 
Pretty good, especially the main menu music. But not memorable. Just nice BGM. Not really worth paying for the OST imo but who am i to decide.

For me the games strong points are the art direction or visual direction in combination with the player interacting with the desktop. It really immerses you in your role as the operator and you really feel like you are investigating CCTV footage and sifting through documents to find small clues. The game really takes you out of this illusion by having to click the objective and then clicking the requested information. Not a fan of that, could have been integrated in a more smooth and immersive way. Audio design is great too, the voice acting feels believable enough and the sound effects are accurate and synced well. Nothing really to complain about there.

Overall it is a fun, short and interesting game with a few flaws that can be overlooked. Wait for a sale before you buy it though, for 3-4 hours of playtime it is just a bit too much (About 1€/$ per hour of playtime should be standard imo).

I enjoyed the game and, right up until its ending, I was sad that it was about to end.

The ending killed it for me. It wasn't a bad twist, it was how forced of a tragic ending it was. If you don't mind spoilers, see below:

[spoiler] Everybody dies. Well, okay, one person is on the run from the law and another is imprisoned for life, but everybody else dies with extra fluff added to the details of what happened to twist the knife even harder that, after everything you did throughout the game, it was all meaningless because you failed. Might as well have had Patrick Star read me the extended cut of the Ugly Barnacle.[/spoiler]

The intensity of the tragic ending was so dramatic, I went online so I could see what I did to get the bad ending because it gave me such bad whiplash. Nope, no bad ending. Just one ending. It didn't earn or build up to leaving me holding an empty bag of misery. It has extra secrets, but because its ending left me feeling the way it did, I don't feel like I have any reason to TRY and learn more. It doesn't feel like there's a point to learning more outside of satisfying the curiosity I was feeling right up until the game kicked me in the crotch.

If you don't mind stories that abruptly end tragically, literally everything else about the game felt solid. I almost want to give this a recommendation. However, with the ending leaving me feel like nothing was accomplished but a few hours burned down the hole, I feel like I can only recommend this with "Play it at your own risk."

review_text_raw:
Overall, I adored this game.  I struggle with this next phrase because i don't fully mean it and understand why it is the way it is... but I'm glad I bought it on sale and not full price as it's not quite worth the full price.  I mostly say this due to game length and lack of choice in endings.  I took a look and it looks like this might be a first time game from this dev, who I'm guessing is solo or very small which is VERY exciting to see if this is their freshman showing.

Things I LOVED:
-Dynamic story telling.  There was a clear storyline running through from start to finish.  Not overly convoluted, not too cliche or simple.  Were the twists a little predictable?  Maybe a few.  But that didn't take away from the impact when they hit anyway.  The pacing of those drops were excellently done.
-Style was lovely.  I REALLY dug the overall look of the game.  The various tools you got to us, the puzzles you go to solve... all from a single terminal.  It made me think of a hacking game from the early 00s of gaming sites that I loved to play over and over.
-The voice acting was excellent.  Really stellar work.
-The game itself.  It's just really enjoyable.  It was well paced, the mystery was fun, the story was easy to follow, the puzzles were a bit easy but a few had some real challenges in there.  One puzzle was a bit too much of a lateral thinking puzzle, BUT that was one of the best twists of the whole game so I can overlook it. 

Things I wish were different (not bad, just things I wanted more of):
-it's far too short.  It took me about 4 hours to complete and that was going very slow and taking my time, looking at my phone a lot and doing a few other things at the same time. (thanks ADHD)  The story telling and plot that the game is driving could easily have been a full scale game.  And I'd pay good money for it, too.  This is top notch story telling from a new dev and I hope we see more.
-Lack of use of cool tools.  You're introduced to several cool mini puzzles throughout the game like a car analyzer, a bomb diffuser, and chemical component analyzer.  All of them have robust rules and options with them.  And they're all used only once.  You gave us so many cool toys.. let us play with them!!
-No story diversity with a [spoiler] really weak and bad ending [/spoiler].  While the story they have given is lovely, your choices don't matter.  There is just that ending.  I wanted more options, i wanted to affect the story with how i played and wanted the game reward cleverness (i.e. if you found a certain name on a certain list before you were told to.)

All that being said, if you like mystery games, if you like hack style games, this is a great choice.  I am very excited to see what this dev does in the future.  If this is their first showing, we are in for some real gems in the future!!

review_text_raw:
Yet another case where a "neutral" review option would be a great feature on steam.

The Operator is somewhat summed up as an detective esk simulator game where the bulk of the gamelay loop is behind your desk, gathering evidence & solving cases by connecting the dots. It was clearly inspired by games such as Orwell: Keeping An Eye On You, Song of Farca and the likes, so if that's up your alley you'll most likely also enjoy this one.

Though: an unfortunate difference between those games and this one is both the depth & usage of the built in systems/tools at your disposal, the very linear story, and the playtime of the game. Starting with the latter, a normal playthrough of the game sits around 2 to 3 hours. As the game is very linear in terms of choices you can make (the choices only change a few minor responses, there is only a singular ending and your choices don't affect this) there is not really a great reason to replay the game unless you're going for all achievements; as some are missable on a first playthrough.

Which makes the price, +-14EUR (without sale, as of writing this), a complicated point.

Apart from the playtime, the game makes up for it by the amazing voice acting (not AI generated), _amazing_ polished look and feel (you can clearly see a lot of love and thought were poured into this) and really interesting scenes (artistic direction wise) splattered between days. All in all, really good experience and amazing opener; especially for an indie developer. (there are some minor complaints such as the chat stealing your focus when having to make a choice preventing you from typing in a different window, but nothing game breaking.) -- Just in the end wished with this much work & love put into it, the story was a tad longer.

My final gripe was the somewhat limited use and complexity of the tools given to you. It goes hand in hand with the point about playtime, because how else would you utilize a lab analysis tool or terminal if not by expanding the story. There were tools that looked really interesting, but are in the end just used once; which is a shame really. The times you do utilize them are fun and all feel unique.

So. All in all, a really solid game that I see more so as a foundation for something bigger. It at times feels more like a demo than an full game story wise. If you don't mind the price for what you're getting, and games like orwell are up your alley; you'll enjoy this one. But it may be better to wait for the operator 2 (which is currently in development!) or play a similar game if you're looking for a longer story or if you don't prefer the linear story style of this game.


In the end I'd give it a 6.5/10. Absolutely loved what it had, but left me wanting more. Wunderforce described it perfectly in another review: "Clearly the quality is top-notch but it's a bit baffling someone would put so much work into something so short. This makes it almost feel like a long demo."

I'm only giving this a thumbs down because I believe this is marketed incorrectly. I loved the game for what it is, a visual novel. But this is not necessarily a detective game, and I'd argue not even really investigative.
The game follows one story line, and kind of fools you into thinking your choices matter when they really don't. For example, I attempted every dialogue option to not work with HAL, but that didn't matter, I had to work with them anyway.
The tools used are awesome; facial recognition, Human Database, lab analysis. But we only use some of these things once or a few times at most.
Don't get me wrong, the story is fantastic, and I genuinely loved my time with it. I agree with a lot of the other reviews that this should be way longer, but overall, I think the game is marketed incorrectly which is where I can't recommend it. I, and it seems a lot of others, went into this with the idea I would be solving multiple cases, using the technology multiple times, maybe even an endless mode where there's multiple variations of possible cases. 
I do think it's a great game, the immersion into the FDI computer is fantastic, the art style/graphics are perfect, everything ran smoothly. I mean genuinely top marks across (most of) the board. But it did leave me wanting more, I really dislike that we only used some of the tools once, and my choices didn't matter. All that being said, I absolutely would purchase another game from this dev.

review_text_raw:
A great game had it come out about a decade ago. There's nothing the game does that other games don't do in greater depth and with greater innovation and interest. Tools and mechanics are all used at a very basic level, and there's no integration of multiple tools or strategies on a case to reach a conclusion as in other games of this genre. 
For example, a truly innovative element of the game is the use of a spectrometer tool, wherein information on a sample must be looked up and entered precisely in order to derive lab results. However, the tool is only used a single time. Other games in this genre would have made it a permanent element of the game moving forward, integrating it alongside other tools and resources to solve cases. This game uses it once, then abandons the idea entirely.
There's a bomb defusal scene which is fantastic... until you realize that the information is static rather than being generated. The plot and story are ok, with some nods to the X-Files and 90s conspiracies along the way, but again nothing really new or innovative beyond what's already been done in similar games. 

In sum, this is a great demo for a game that came out in 2013, but better, more complete, more elaborate, more creative games already exist that do the same things.

review_text_raw:
TL;DR
Overall a solid, if short, experience. If you like games similar to Killer Frequency, Hypnospace Outlaw, or even Papers Please, you will enjoy this. I felt the story was paced well enough and presented well enough to keep my interest to the end. My only complaints are the length of the game, a lack of content, and I had the story fairly well figured out before the climax. The puzzles were well put together, for the most part, but none of them felt difficult and I completed them pretty quickly, and enjoyed doing so. For 15$ I think it's worth your time if you're looking for a few hours to kill doing detective work. On sale I definitely recommend it.

GAMEPLAY:
The gameplay is pretty simplistic. As stated above similar to the likes of Hypnospace Outlaw where you navigate a computer system using different apps and given information (files) to solve puzzles. The puzzles themselves I felt weren't overly difficult, but done well enough to definitely have me pay more attention to various things. They also do a great job with handling a few very important plot points in the game. One section, in particular, did get me rather anxious. Overall it does its job well, and I enjoyed pretty much all of it. The only problem I had overall with gameplay was the lack of content. It gives you some interesting tools to utilize, then just sort of forgets about them.

SOUND:
I really enjoyed what they did with this game. The music really fit the moments and added some flair to various points in the game. The ambient sound and environmental sounds are also done VERY well to play parts in the game. It may not blow your mind, but I appreciate the amount of effort they put forth in this front. The soundtrack is quite good.

STORY:
They do a good job giving a good detective story to play out. You may or may not figure out the twists and turns it will take. Unfortunately I had some of the big reveals pegged within the first hour. On the other hand, I still enjoyed it enough to keep going. It won't blow your mind or take you into the depths of the universe they created; it gives you what it needs to, and executes it well. I don't care if a story blows my mind, so long as I have fun experiencing it, which I did here.

As a side note for the story, they did do a great job with a few moments of making them actually very tense. My only complaint, as stated above, is that it felt too short.


IN CONCLUSION:
The Operator is a solid entry into this detective-like puzzle-solving Operating System-simulator genre. I enjoyed my time with it, I do enjoy the mechanics of utilizing a computer in game to solve various puzzles with information that is available, but you have to search for. While sort, it didn't overstay its welcome and accomplished what it set out to do. I will greatly look forward to another game of this style if they decide to do one!

review_text_raw:
(This review contains information that might be considered spoilers for some, so read with caution!)

TL; DR:
It holds your hand throughout the game. The investigative puzzles are immersive, but simple and provides very little challenge. It's short, but you might possible still like it for it's presentation and story. If there was a "lukewarm" rating, I would pick that. But since it's clearly a labor of love, I'm inclined to rate positively.

The longer review:

When I heard of The Operator a few days before launch, I was hoping for something to scratch that Obra Dinn / Curse of the Golden Idol itch. Not very many games manage to make you feel like a proper investigator or makes you feel super clever when you progress, and those two games are the gold standard.

The Operator - unfortunately - is not that game.

The immersion is great. You definitely feel like an operator, scanning photos for details that you then input into various databases to yield result. The interface is exactly how you'd imagine a 90's 'hacker' terminal to look like, complete with a terminal and an official looking 'FBI' interface. The majority of the game is fully voiced with competent actors (for the budget).

Although a very polished and - for its medium - a cinematic experience, gameplay-wise it falls into many of the same pitfalls as other "investigative" games like it. The puzzles are - for the most part, but with notable exceptions - simple, requiring few steps to solve. Your hand is woefully held through each of them and the freedom to make your own deductions are sorely lacking. For the most part the tools required to solve a certain puzzle will appear when needed, and disappear when not needed anymore.

The story is decent and very on-par for such a game. It doesn't fully manage to suck you into the world, however. For one, the main plot felt rushed. You're a new operator working cases, and the very first case you receive is a part of a brewing conspiracy. Every case following that is connected in some way. In my opinion, the game doesn't take it's time to build up the world or the characters before placing you front and center into the main plot thread. 

Some of the major plot twists are extremely predictable, and some of what is presented as a major plot development honestly really isn't. We don't know the involved characters enough to care when the revelation is given to us.
The game also makes the cardinal sin of ending abruptly with no real resolution, most questions left unanswered and a feeling that your actions throughout the game had little impact.

A lot of this comes down to personal tastes, hopes and expectations, however. Chances are you'll like this game for it's good presentation and decent enough puzzles. It's not particularly expensive (though maybe a bit pricey for the estimated game time).

Not very many games manage to make you feel like a proper investigator or makes you feel super clever when you progress, and those two games are the gold standard. The Operator - unfortunately - is not that game. The immersion is great. You definitely feel like an operator, scanning photos for details that you then input into various databases to yield result. The interface is exactly how you'd imagine a 90's 'hacker' terminal to look like, complete with a terminal and an official looking 'FBI' interface. The majority of the game is fully voiced with competent actors (for the budget). Although a very polished and - for its medium - a cinematic experience, gameplay-wise it falls into many of the same pitfalls as other "investigative" games like it. The puzzles are - for the most part, but with notable exceptions - simple, requiring few steps to solve. Your hand is woefully held through each of them and the freedom to make your own deductions are sorely lacking. For the most part the tools required to solve a certain puzzle will appear when needed, and disappear when not needed anymore. The story is decent and very on-par for such a game. It doesn't fully manage to suck you into the world, however. For one, the main plot felt rushed. You're a new operator working cases, and the very first case you receive is a part of a brewing conspiracy. Every case following that is connected in some way. In my opinion, the game doesn't take it's time to build up the world or the characters before placing you front and center into the main plot thread. Some of the major plot twists are extremely predictable, and some of what is presented as a major plot development honestly really isn't. We don't know the involved characters enough to care when the revelation is given to us. The game also makes the cardinal sin of ending abruptly with no real resolution, most questions left unanswered and a feeling that your actions throughout the game had little impact. A lot of this comes down to personal tastes, hopes and expectations, however. Chances are you'll like this game for it's good presentation and decent enough puzzles. It's not particularly expensive (though maybe a bit pricey for the estimated game time).

Aesthetically pleasing, good story with at the very least, decent voice acting if not great. Runs well. An interesting gameplay mechanic that has you sitting at your desk, putting together pieces of the puzzles as agents sweep the field for evidence and follow the leads you help develop. The story has you unraveling a conspiracy, using computer tools, metadata, and analyzing software to pull the narrative together. It's fascinating, and the game does a really good job at making you feel like you're truly a professional analyst, solving crimes from the comfort of a desk in Washington DC.

Problem is, the game is pretty darn short. Only about 4 hours of gameplay, and it feels deeply on rails, to the point that the puzzle portion of it feels more like a addon to the rest of the game. If you subscribe to the $1 per hour mindset, even discounted to $9, this game is technically not worth it, as the game has limited replayability. Though, the game does make up for it with the story and gameplay to a degree. It is, at the very least, a pretty impactful 4 hours, and you could get somewhat different results if you repeat the story, so there is a small sense that your choices matter. 

I might just be spoiled, coming off of The Roottrees are Dead which had a fairly similar premise of using a computer to uncover information that can fill in the blanks. But in TRaD, they introduce you to the tools and then you spend a bulk of the time using them on your own to fill in profiles on the family tree. There was a lot more blanks to fill in and time to spend fiddling around with information. With TO, you get introduced to cool mechanics and tools on your computer, and then use almost none of them ever again. The game feels like a 4 hour tutorial other than the story, which takes interesting turns and, as a flipside, keeps the player continously faced with new and interesting problems to solve. It sucks not being able to repeatedly use a mechanic I got familiar with or a handbook I just learned, but every in-game day pulls me straight in with a curveball, gameplay wise or story wise.

The ending kinda left a bad taste in my mouth. AFAIK, your choices don't really seem to affect the ending from what I saw online in guides and gameplay.

Still gonna leave it as a positive review, because I quite enjoyed this and I think the devs are absolutely cooking here. I just hope the developers consider putting more meat on the bones of TO2, because it feels like there is a ton of potential for a truly great puzzle/detective game here that only gets partially realized.

This is an excellent, short puzzle and story game as an Operator in the FDI assisting agents with cases

The game opens with a cut scene which you watch and this sets the tone. Then you see a computer terminal boot up and you log in. This is the start of your job as an operator for the FDI (Federal Department of Intelligence). This is the main screen you see and involves taking calls, running through evidence and assisting agents with their cases.

There is a small cast of characters – you assist a few agents, you hear from the director, who is a friend, and you have a direct supervisor. There are also a couple of other people you hear from. To start with the calls walk you through the basics of the set up and the mechanics you will be using. Then you are given your first call from an agent.

The element of “assisting” agents is fun and about solving puzzles. Finding people in databases, working out how to get evidence from clues in video and audio files and some careful reading of instructions and asking questions. I found the puzzles varied, fun, hard (but not too hard) and appropriate to the setting. The difficulty curve generally increases as the game progresses.

The other people are interesting and I generally liked them, particularly the agents. They were varied, plausible and interesting. There were a couple of dialogue choices where I would have not chosen from the options given, but mostly they were plausible too.

The progression of the different cases builds the stories, tone and difficulty of the puzzles. Also, the puzzles generally get harder, although one or two of the later ones are still quite quick. 

Video and audio are basic but effective, this isn't a high budget game but makes excellent use of what it has.

Saving happens when you exit the game, this isn't particularly clear to start with. I think the rule is that if you are between cases then you just save, but if you are in the middle of a call, then it will take you back to the start of the call/case. Which has the advantage of letting you return to the game and not be in the middle of something complicated, it is also something you can use if you want another attempt at a puzzle (as you can fail some of them).

I won't say too much about the ending. There is only one ending (confirmed by the game designer) and it does seem a little sequel-hook like. Also, there is a post credits scene.

In general, this is a really interesting puzzle story game and be aware of it's comparatively short length.

When I played the demo for The Operator, I knew I was onto something special. I gave it a spin on release day and liked it so much I did a second run-through to pick up all the pieces I missed and see the alternate paths I didn't take the first time.

The Operator's premise is simple; you're an operator for the FDI who handles agent's queries. An agent on the ground will send you photos and videos of what they're seeing, and you have to find the information the agent wants. This includes finding the data or the discrepancy and clicking on it, Papers Please style. And your first day doesn't even finish before something seriously odd starts happening.

The Operator comes in at 3-4 hours of playtime, with an extra hour or two if you decide to replay for all the tidbits like I did. At its price point, some people may dislike that it doesn't hold up to the golden ratio of "one dollar for one hour of game time." Fortunately, this game proves the positive side of the adage "you get what you pay for," because it's by no means an ordinary game.

From the excellent story, to the gripping twists, to the fully voiced characters and the brain-melting puzzles, The Operator is well worth the asking price. My absolute favourite part of the game is its sound design; there are musical stings when evidence appears, and little ramp-ups when a case progresses. My fave parts in the game happened because the game detected that I'm on the right track with solving a puzzle and ramped up the music in response. It gives an incredible cinematic feel that makes you feel like you're in a movie.

I understand that most people will probably feel uneasy paying what the developer asks to get 3-4 hours of gameplay, and if that's you, I recommend wishlisting and coming back when it's on sale. But if you can bite the bullet, you'll find that the game will be more than happy to make every last cent worthwhile.

[b]IF YOU LIKE THIS, TRY:[/b] Home Safety Hotline
This game shares a similar length, premise, and price of another fave of mine; Home Safety Hotline. While The Operator builds on suspense, thrill, and high-stake moments, Home Safety Hotline is surreal, fantastical, and even a little but humorous. As such, if The Operator leaves you wanting more, I recommend this one, too.

Reviewing (mostly) every game (or DLC) in my library, part 98:

⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️☆☆ (8/10)

[i] The Operator [/i] casts you not as a hero in the field, but as the analyst—the voice behind the computer—supporting agents from the shadows. It’s a fascinating setup and a fresh twist on crime-solving games, and usually almost always lives up to its potential!

🖥[b] Pros: [/b]
[list]
[*] Authentic "operator" fantasy. You monitor missions from your desk, field phone calls, look through mysterious documents, and scrub through CCTV footage. 

[*] Diverse tools. The game gives you a chem scanner, facial recognition database, image enhancement tech, and document search systems. For example, in one mission, you identify a suspect by cross-referencing a blurry security camera with an equally blurry security footage of his car and license plate. That kind of detective work feels cool. You feel smart when it works.

[*] Great use of puzzles under pressure. A standout moment has you guiding a field agent through bomb defusal. You have to analyze chemicals, check your reference files, and read out step-by-step instructions—all while the timer ticks down. These time-sensitive missions are where the game shines.

[*] Well-done audio design. The UI clicks, radio static, and phone calls all contribute to a grounded, late-'90s thriller vibe. The voice acting is low-key but sells the scenario well, especially during moments of stress or confusion.

[*] No filler. It’s tight and focused. No wandering, no padding. You’re thrown into the action quickly and missions move at a brisk pace.
[/list]

[b]🧾 Cons: [/b]
[list]
[*] Flat characters. The field agents and mysterious hacker HAL are more archetypes than flesh-and-blood. They push the story forward, but rarely surprise

[*] Choices don’t matter much. There are dialogue branches, but most are cosmetic. Whether you’re professional or snarky, or even whether you succeed or fail at certain puzzles, the game mostly funnels you into the same story beats.

[*] Abrupt ending. The game ends just as things get interesting. HAL’s storyline ramps up, then vanishes. You barely get to dig into the conspiracy or see the consequences of your actions. It feels like a miniseries that ends on episode three.
[/list]

Unfortunate to release a game like this in-between the Golden Idol game, as it makes look like it could a smilar type of investigation game. This is not really the case, even though you could really batch it with it and Obra Dinn as point & click made for people prejudicied against point & click, The Operator have more stronger emphasis on its narrative over the actual case solving.

This probably no biggest departure between what you could expect compared to what the game delivers so it's probably what needs to be the clearest : this isn't some X-files case solving about solving stranges cases and chasing aliens, this is short narrative game. While I kinda wish it had more filler cases, that would require to use all the different tools to solve, it's clearly outside the scope of this game. The story itself is a very typical thriller, to the point is possible to get where it's trying to go just because the trope used are that common and maybe it would a problem if this was a visual novel.

The obvious gimmick here is the entire game is told through the screen of a computer, a very limited dispositive that get the most out of the very conventional plot. This may sound dismissive thriller are very codified type of story, that's part of the interest in even saying "this is a thriller", the same way I expect to see a group of young people sharing their sob stories and their way to save the world in my J-RPG. So how do you make something like this interesting when you can't hire Keanu Reeves to do cool stuff on screen ? What the Operator does is giving as little as possible. Low quality camera footage, damaged photography, unreliable testimony, chat windows and a lot of phone calls, an quick acces to a lot clues but very little interaction with the actual narrative. Backed-up by the dynamic soundtrack, this game creates some pretty sincere moment of tension. Especially when the main character position matches the player playing the game, good for immersion even if you don't emphasize too much with the character (I didn't really, sorry).

I do think this game overall is a bit short and lack a bit of substance as an investigation game, but is a narrative game really dedicated to its theme.

This probably no biggest departure between what you could expect compared to what the game delivers so it's probably what needs to be the clearest : this isn't some X-files case solving about solving stranges cases and chasing aliens, this is short narrative game. While I kinda wish it had more filler cases, that would require to use all the different tools to solve, it's clearly outside the scope of this game. The story itself is a very typical thriller, to the point is possible to get where it's trying to go just because the trope used are that common and maybe it would a problem if this was a visual novel. The obvious gimmick here is the entire game is told through the screen of a computer, a very limited dispositive that get the most out of the very conventional plot. This may sound dismissive thriller are very codified type of story, that's part of the interest in even saying "this is a thriller", the same way I expect to see a group of young people sharing their sob stories and their way to save the world in my J-RPG. So how do you make something like this interesting when you can't hire Keanu Reeves to do cool stuff on screen ? What the Operator does is giving as little as possible. Low quality camera footage, damaged photography, unreliable testimony, chat windows and a lot of phone calls, an quick acces to a lot clues but very little interaction with the actual narrative. Backed-up by the dynamic soundtrack, this game creates some pretty sincere moment of tension. Especially when the main character position matches the player playing the game, good for immersion even if you don't emphasize too much with the character (I didn't really, sorry). I do think this game overall is a bit short and lack a bit of substance as an investigation game, but is a narrative game really dedicated to its theme.

An amazing game with deep plot, mostly unexpected plot twists and an amazing style, ruined by only one terrible ending, unskippable end-of-day cutscenes, and NO SAVING.

The single ending in this game is the biggest "fuck you," you could ever give to someone. They build up such good tension, make you feel like you have a choice just to rip it all away in one lame ending where basically, "bad guy wins, your friends all die." Don't bother getting invested in this wonderful story, because the ending undoes all of what they built.

Also the game is literally only 3 hours, just enough to not refund. and for $20?!? This is a game I'd say is worth 5 dollars if you even liked it. Only get on steep discount, and if you hate yourself.
